title: India-US Trade Pact in Legal Drafting, Held for Competitive Edge
excerpt: Goyal says the first tranche is finalised, but New Delhi will operationalise it only once exporters gain an advantage over Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia.
body:
• The first tranche of the India-US bilateral trade agreement has been finalised and is now in legal drafting, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday, October 15.
  • New Delhi will operationalise the pact only once Indian exporters secure a comparable or competitive advantage over peer countries such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia in the US market.
  • Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal linked the signing timetable to Washington formalising its overall tariff structure and outcomes under Section 301.
  • Goyal also set a timeline for the parallel India-EU deal: signing in December, with entry into force in February or March 2027.

India and the United States have finished negotiating the first tranche of their bilateral trade agreement and moved it into legal drafting, but New Delhi will not put it into operation until Indian exporters are assured a tariff edge over rival suppliers to the US market. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal made the condition explicit on Thursday at an event in New Delhi, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

"The first tranche has been finalised and it is going through final contours, the legal drafting."

— Piyush Goyal, Commerce and Industry Minister

What Is New in This Statement

Earlier updates this week centred on momentum — that major items had been cleared and that talks were nearing a landing point. Goyal's remarks add two concrete elements that were not in those accounts. First, the text has moved from negotiation to legal drafting, the stage at which agreed language is turned into a signable document. Second, operationalisation is now publicly tied to a test: whether the final tariff lines give India a comparable or competitive advantage over its peer countries. Reporting by The Daily Jagran, drawing on Reuters, identified those peers as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia — the economies Indian exporters most directly compete with for US orders in garments, footwear and light manufacturing.

Why the Competitive-Advantage Test Matters

A deal that merely restores earlier access would not be enough for New Delhi. Under the framework the two sides agreed in February, punitive US tariffs on most Indian goods were brought down to 18 per cent from 50 per cent, after an earlier round of talks collapsed in August last year. If competitors end up with lower effective rates, Indian suppliers could still lose orders despite a signed pact. That is why the government is framing the finish line in relative terms, not just as a signing date.

The stakes are visible in the trade numbers. India's goods exports to the United States rose to $42.79 billion in April-August, from $40.39 billion a year earlier, and India recorded a trade surplus of nearly $34 billion with the United States in fiscal 2025/26. For exporters and for Indian professionals whose employers sell into the US market, even a few percentage points of tariff difference can decide where the next contract is placed.

The Washington Side of the Timetable

Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations were moving in the right direction and that India anticipated closing and signing the deal at the earliest possible time. He added a condition on the US side: the pact has to be signed when the overall tariff structure is formalised in the United States, with parallel work under way there and progress linked in part to outcomes under Section 301. Neither side has publicly detailed all the reasons for the delay, and a new US law that could open the way to steep additional tariffs linked to India's purchases of Russian oil remains a complicating factor in the background.

A Second Track: The European Union

Goyal also updated the parallel European track. He said the free trade agreement between India and the European Union will be inked in December and would come into force from February or March next year. Running the US and EU negotiations together gives Indian exporters two major-market openings within months of each other, and gives New Delhi leverage to compare the terms on offer in each.

What to Watch Next

The next milestones are the completion of legal drafting, clarity on the US tariff structure Agrawal cited, and a mutually agreed signing date. Until the tariff schedules are published, exporters cannot price the deal's benefit precisely. Readers should watch for the text's treatment of the sectors where India competes head-to-head with Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia, because Goyal has now made that comparison the public test of whether the pact is ready to operate.
